### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Odle, Duke, and Dunens build a transparent three-part screen on public data — a 2019–20 Pell six-year graduation rate above the sample median of 50% with a Pell/non-Pell gap below the median 13 points (584 institutions pass), an ACE/Carnegie SAEC Earnings Ratio of at least 1.54, the 75th percentile (349 pass), and a 2019–20 Pell graduation rate above the value predicted by an OLS model trained on 2015–16 through 2018–19 (829 of 1,462 pass, i.e., any positive residual) — and publish the 149 four-year institutions that clear all three, with data and code deposited at openICPSR (p.6; Table 2, pp.8–9; p.13). That inventory, the explicit rule that generated it, and the early use of the 2025 SAEC measures are real contributions, and readers can rely on them as a descriptive product: the sample arithmetic (1,640 − 14 − 164 = 1,462; 1,462 × 5 = 7,310), the Table 2 count (exactly 149; 47 public, 99 private nonprofit, 3 for-profit), and every number transcribed from Tables 1 and 3 into the prose check out. The problem is that the paper's own description of what it found does not match its exhibits, and the most quotable sentences are the least supported. The abstract says HPPs have "low access and attainment gaps" (p.1), Figure 1 (p.4) brackets the whole framework with "Equitable Access: Serving similar shares of Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients," and the conceptual model promises institutions that "enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students" (pp.4–5) — yet none of the three operational criteria measures access, and Table 1 (p.7) shows the average HPP enrolls fewer Pell students than its geography predicts (Pell Ratio 0.77; 24.5% Pell versus a stated 38% sample average), while Table 3 (p.10) makes the Pell Ratio the strongest negative predictor of HPP status (β = −0.150, SE 0.022). The list is two-thirds private nonprofit, 59% doctoral, includes Harvard, MIT, Stanford, Princeton, Cornell, and Chicago, and contains no CUNY campus; "diverse" is true only in the weak sense that a handful of broad-access publics (three CSU campuses, UC Merced, FIU, FAMU, Houston, Rutgers–Camden) also pass. The second headline — that traditional quantitative measures "do a poor job" of explaining HPP status (adjusted R² = 0.218 versus 0.658 for the graduation-rate model), so unobserved validating cultures "likely drive" it (pp.10–11) — is partly built into the design, because criterion 3 is itself a residual from a model on largely the same covariates, and no selectivity variable appears anywhere despite p.2 naming "admissions rates" among the measures tested. The right posture is therefore: use the screen and the inventory, quote the criteria from p.6 and the numbers from the tables, and set aside the access, diversity, and culture claims until someone re-runs the screen with an access floor, a selectivity control, Pell-specific earnings, and a multi-year stability check — all of which the paper itself lists as future work (p.12). This sits at the boundary with "Treat with Caution"; it stays on the "Useful" side because the central deliverable is checkable and the deposit exists, not because the interpretive claims hold up.

#### Key Strengths

- A fully stated, reproducible classification rule with explicit cutoffs and pass counts at each stage (50% / 13 points / 1.54 / positive residual; 584 / 349 / 829 / 149; p.6), a complete inventory naming all 149 institutions with state and control (Table 2, pp.8–9), and a declared data-and-code deposit with a persistent identifier (https://doi.org/10.3886/E248577V1, p.13). For a descriptive typology built entirely on public IPEDS and SAEC files, these are the conditions under which full replication is realistic.
- Internal arithmetic and transcription are clean. Sample flow (1,640 − 14 − 164 = 1,462), the missingness denominator (1,640 × 5 × 46 = 377,200), the panel count (1,462 × 5 = 7,310), Table 2's row count and control split (47/99/3 → 31.54% public, matching Table 1), and all 18 Table 1 and 8 Table 3 values quoted in the Results match the exhibits, with financial units correctly rescaled.
- One of the first peer-reviewed applications of the 2025 ACE/Carnegie Student Access and Earnings Classification, showing how to join its Pell, URM, and Earnings ratios to the post-2015 IPEDS Pell graduation panel (pp.4–5). The data novelty is real even where the conceptual novelty is oversold.
- Candid boundary-setting in the notes and policy section: the SAEC earnings measure is not intergenerational mobility and covers all Title IV entrants rather than Pell recipients (note 4, p.13); SAEC geographic coverage varies (note 10); 164 unclassified institutions are dropped for stated reasons (note 11); the panel stops pre-COVID by design (note 7); and the authors explicitly warn against accountability uses of the framework (p.12).
- A genuine existence result survives the caveats: some broad-access, higher-Pell public institutions — CSU Fresno, San Bernardino, and Stanislaus; UC Merced; Florida International; Florida A&M; University of Houston; Rutgers–Camden — clear a demanding joint completion-gap-earnings screen (Table 2). That is citable and is a reasonable sampling frame for the qualitative case studies the paper calls for.

#### Key Concerns

- **Access is claimed throughout but never operationalized, and the data point the other way.** The abstract ("low access and attainment gaps," p.1), Figure 1 ("Equitable Access" bracket, p.4), the conceptual model ("enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students," pp.4–5), the LPM description ("achieving high access," p.6), and the Conclusion ("excel in access," p.12) all describe an access dimension absent from the three criteria on p.6. HPPs' mean Pell Ratio is 0.77 and their Pell share 24.5% against a stated 38% sample average (Table 1, p.7; p.6), and the Pell Ratio is the single strongest negative predictor of HPP status (−0.150***, Table 3, p.10). The text reports the adjacent URM Ratio (0.97) but never mentions the Pell Ratio row. A reader who takes "High Performing Pell" to mean "serves many low-income students well" will be misled; it means "serves its relatively few Pell students well on these metrics."

  > **Correction (2026-09-25).** The sentence above says the text never mentions the Pell Ratio row of Table 3. That is wrong. Page 10 states that the likelihood of HPP status "falls by 15.0 percentage points" per one-unit increase in the Pell Ratio, and page 11 discusses the negative association. What the prose does not connect to the access claim is Table 1's descriptive Pell Ratio (0.77) and 24.5% Pell share. The abstract's "low access ... gaps" claim, which no criterion measures, stands. Found during comparison with the independent Codex review; confirmed against the rendered page.

- **The "traditional measures explain little, so culture matters" argument is partly mechanical and omits the obvious predictor.** Criterion 3 is a positive residual from a model of Pell graduation rates on institutional features; the LPM then regresses HPP status on largely the same features (p.6; p.10, "these same measures"). A status defined in part as being unexplained by these covariates will, to that extent, be poorly explained by them, and an adjusted R² of 0.218 for a binary outcome with a roughly 10% base rate is not low by ordinary standards. No admissions rate, test score, or other selectivity variable appears on p.5 or in Table 3, although p.2 lists "admissions rates" among the measures shown to explain HPP status poorly. The Discussion's inference that institutions "do not become HPPs by simply increasing spending or enrolling different students" (p.11) is a hypothesis, not a finding — and Table 3's two largest coefficients (Pell Ratio −0.150, Doctoral +0.145) say that enrolling different students and being a particular kind of institution are exactly what correlates with HPP status.
- **The Discussion contradicts the Results, and several "findings" restate the selection rule.** Results (p.10) calls student demographics and doctoral status "statistically significant and meaningful predictors"; the Discussion (p.11) says "student demographics, and Carnegie classifications — have limited explanatory power." The p.6 comparisons (76.5% vs. a 50% median; 1.89 vs. 1.35; 3.80 vs. 13 points) compare HPP means with sample medians on the very variables HPPs were selected on — they verify the filter, they are not evidence. The prose also names "the share of students awarded Pell grants" as a predictor (p.10) when Table 3 contains only the geography-relative Pell Ratio.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The two statements are compatible and p. 10 draws the distinction. "Meaningful predictor" describes coefficient size (Doctoral +0.145***, Pell Ratio −0.150*** in Table 3); "limited explanatory power" describes variance explained, which is small (Doctoral accounts for at most 5.7% of the variation in HPP status). The Discussion does not contradict the Results on this point. The rest of the bullet, that the p. 6 comparisons verify the selection filter rather than test anything, stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

- **The classification is single-year, knife-edge, and untested for stability, with its key step in an unavailable appendix.** Criteria 1 and 3 rest on one year (2019–20); criterion 3 counts any positive residual (56.7% of the sample) yet the Discussion speaks of campuses that "substantially outperform" expectations (p.11); no sensitivity to thresholds, no criterion overlaps, and no uncertainty are reported; and the prediction model's predictor set, functional form, and R² of 0.658 (p.10) live only in the Online Appendix, so a reader cannot tell whether lagged graduation rates are predictors — which would turn "performance in context" into "year-over-year change." Table 3's structure (a time-invariant 2019–20 indicator stacked on five years of covariates with year fixed effects, title "2019–21" against a 2015–16 through 2019–20 source line) is never explained.
- **The literature the method actually belongs to is missing, and the novelty claims are inflated.** "Actual versus predicted graduation rate" exemplar-finding (Astin; Kuh et al.'s Project DEEP; Education Trust; the college value-added literature) and combined access-completion-earnings frameworks (Chetty et al.'s mobility rates; the Postsecondary Value Commission) are not cited, so the known pitfalls of residual rankings — noise at small institutions, regression to the mean, selection contaminating residuals — go unmentioned. Note 6's claim that earnings has been "absent from prior work in this area" is not right; the paper's real novelty is the SAEC data. Critiques of Pell status as a cross-institution low-income proxy, and the selection-versus-effect literature that bears on reading Harvard's or MIT's earnings ratio as institutional performance, are also absent. Kelchen (2017), one of three named pillars, is a Brookings blog post, and the "Kelchen classification" on p.6 appears to be the authors' own operationalization.

#### What to Rely On

- The operational definition of an HPP, taken from p.6 only: Pell six-year graduation rate above 50% and Pell/non-Pell gap below 13 points in 2019–20; SAEC Earnings Ratio ≥ 1.54; and a 2019–20 Pell graduation rate above an OLS prediction trained on 2015–16 through 2018–19. Pass counts 584, 349, 829; joint 149 of 1,462.
- The inventory itself (Table 2, pp.8–9): 149 institutions, 47 public, 99 private nonprofit, 3 for-profit (Chamberlain–Ohio, DigiPen, West Coast University–LA), with the Table 1 profile: mean Pell graduation rate 76.54%, non-Pell 80.34%, gap 3.80 points, Earnings Ratio 1.89, Pell Ratio 0.77, 24.52% Pell, 59.06% doctoral, 53.02% highly residential, 0.67% HBCU (one institution), 12.08% land-grant.
- The descriptive fact that a joint high-completion, small-gap, high-earnings screen selects institutions that on average under-enroll Pell students relative to their geographies (Pell Ratio 0.77, Table 1; β = −0.150, Table 3) and that are disproportionately doctoral (β = +0.145) and non-public (β = −0.066). This is the paper's best-supported substantive finding, and it extends the access–success tension in Kelchen (2017) and Wright-Kim et al. (2022) rather than overturning it.
- The existence result: several broad-access publics (CSU Fresno, San Bernardino, Stanislaus; UC Merced; FIU; FAMU; Houston; Rutgers–Camden) pass the screen alongside the elite privates.
- The Table 3 coefficients as descriptive correlates of passing the screen among 1,462 institutions (not 7,310 independent observations): Pell Ratio −0.150***, Doctoral +0.145***, Primarily Non-Residential +0.078**, Public −0.066*, Primarily Residential +0.044*, URM Ratio +0.032*, Average Pell +0.030** per \$1,000, no expenditure variable significant at 5%.
- The sample construction: 1,640 Title IV four-year institutions reporting Pell graduation rates 2015–16 through 2019–20, linear interpolation of 433 of 377,200 cells, 14 dropped for panel gaps, 164 dropped for missing SAEC classification, final N = 1,462; financial variables in 2019 dollars.
- That data and code are declared deposited at openICPSR (DOI 10.3886/E248577V1, p.13) — the DOI resolves (to ICPSR study 248577, V1.0) although the landing page refused an automated fetch, so contents are unconfirmed.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Low access ... gaps" (abstract, p.1) and any statement that HPPs excel in or are selected on access — no access criterion exists (p.6); Table 1's Pell Ratio is 0.77 and Table 3's Pell Ratio coefficient is −0.150.
- "Diverse," "widespread," and "challenges the notion that socioeconomic equity is achieved only within highly resourced or highly selective campus environments" (pp.2, 11, 12) — selectivity is never measured, Table 1 has no non-HPP comparison column, the list is 66% private nonprofit and 59% doctoral, includes six Ivy-Plus institutions, and only about 10% of the sample qualifies; the claim is true only as an existence statement about a handful of regional publics.
- "Traditional quantitative measures do a poor job of explaining this performance" (abstract) and the R² contrast 0.658 vs. 0.218 (p.10) — one criterion is a residual from a model on overlapping covariates, the outcomes are not comparable (continuous vs. thresholded binary at a 10% base rate), and selectivity is omitted; the appendix that would let a reader check the overlap is unavailable.
- "Institutions ... likely become HPPs by developing holistic, proactive, and integrated environments" (p.11) and the ecological-validation attribution — untested; the residual is at least as consistent with unmeasured preparation, selection, and field-of-study mix (which drives the Earnings Ratio at engineering, maritime, and health specialists).
- "Earnings after graduation," "graduates earn," and "High Economic Mobility" (abstract; p.2; Figure 1) — the paper's own quoted SAEC definition (p.5) covers "students who start at a school," 8 years after entry, all Title IV entrants, not Pell graduates and not mobility (note 4); the r = 0.94 Pell/non-Pell program-earnings correlation offered in note 4 has no stated source.
- The p.6 descriptive contrasts (76.5% vs. 50%; 1.89 vs. 1.35; 3.80 vs. 13) — means against medians on the selection variables themselves; the national comparators (38% Pell share, \$4,780 average award, 1.35 median ratio, "roughly 3%" HBCU, "<3%" land-grant) appear in no exhibit.
- The prose sorting of Table 3 predictors into "too small to yield practical significance" versus "meaningful" (p.10) — it follows raw coefficient size, not scaled association: per HPP-sample SD, net price (≈2.7 pp) and percent women (≈3.0 pp) move HPP probability more than Average Pell (≈1.1 pp) or the URM Ratio (≈1.3 pp).
- The Discussion's statement that "Carnegie classifications" have "limited explanatory power" (p.11) — Doctoral is +0.145*** in Table 3 and the Results (p.10) call it meaningful.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** The two statements are compatible and p. 10 draws the distinction. "Meaningful predictor" describes coefficient size (Doctoral +0.145***, Pell Ratio −0.150*** in Table 3); "limited explanatory power" describes variance explained, which is small (Doctoral accounts for at most 5.7% of the variation in HPP status). The Discussion does not contradict the Results on this point. The rest of the bullet, that the p. 6 comparisons verify the selection filter rather than test anything, stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the rendered pages.

- "The share of students awarded Pell grants" and "the number of Pell Grant recipients enrolled" as predictors (p.10) — Table 3 contains only the Pell Ratio, a geography-relative index; the Pell-share variable in Table 1 is the percent of first-year students awarded Pell (p.5), not of all students as p.6 says.
- Any individual institution's membership in Table 2, especially small institutions (36% of HPPs) and any institution near the 50% / 13-point / 1.54 / zero-residual cutoffs — single-year, no uncertainty, no stability check; "substantially outperform" (p.11) describes a rule that requires only a residual above zero.
- The policy recommendation to "direct recognition, resources, and technical support" toward HPPs (p.12) — on the paper's own numbers this would steer resources toward institutions that on average under-enroll Pell students and are often already wealthy; the peer-benchmarking use is the defensible one.
- Table 3's title ("2019–21"), the text's "R² = 0.218" (the table reports adjusted R²), Figure 1's "Wright-Kim et al., 2019" (references say 2022), the Kezar et al. quotation cited to "p. 1" (reference runs pp. 229–242), and the BEA region shares summing to 99.33% — production lapses that survived; quote from the tables.
- Any claim about the prediction model (predictor set, whether lagged graduation rates enter, R² = 0.658, in-sample vs. hold-out) or the LPM specification — all in the unavailable Online Appendix.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)


The paper builds a transparent, rules-based screen that flags 149 "High Performing Pell" (HPP) institutions. An institution has to pass three cutoffs: a completion cutoff, an earnings cutoff, and a better-than-predicted cutoff. The inventory itself is a reasonable descriptive product, as long as readers treat it as the output of particular single-year thresholds. The second headline claim is much weaker. It says that observable institutional traits "do a poor job" of explaining HPP status, and that unobserved campus culture is therefore the likely driver. Part of that result is built into the design, the most obvious traditional predictor (selectivity) is left out, and the design cannot tell culture apart from noise. The paper also presents "access" as a pillar of the framework but never uses it as a selection criterion.

**Strengths:**

- **The classification rule is fully stated and can be reproduced.** Each of the three criteria has an explicit cutoff: a Pell graduation rate above the 50% median plus a Pell/non-Pell gap below 13 points (584 institutions), an Earnings Ratio of 1.54 or higher at the 75th percentile (349), and a positive residual from the prediction model (829), all on p.6. The paper also reports how many institutions pass each criterion alone. Data and code are said to be deposited at https://doi.org/10.3886/E248577V1 (p.13). This review did not examine the deposit.
- **The sample construction is documented and the arithmetic checks out.** The paper starts from 1,640 institutions, drops 14 with an incomplete panel and 164 without SAEC measures, and ends with 1,462 (pp.5–6). Missingness is small: 433 of 377,200 cells (p.5).
- **The paper is candid about its design in several places.** It calls itself exploratory and non-causal (note 9, p.13; p.11, "Rather than attempting causal attribution"). It says openly that Pell graduation rates play "a heavy role in identifying HPPs" (p.6). It stops the panel before COVID (note 7). It notes that the SAEC earnings measure covers all Title IV students, not Pell students specifically (note 4).
- **The inference setup in the LPM is appropriate.** The model pools 1,462 institutions over 5 years (7,310 observations, Table 3, p.10) and clusters standard errors at the institution level (Table 3 note). That is the right choice when a time-invariant designation is repeated across years.
- **The prediction step is set up out of sample.** The model is trained on 2015–16 to 2018–19 and scored on 2019–20 (p.6). That is a sensible way to benchmark "performance in context," though the details could not be checked (see below).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The "low R²" headline is partly produced by the design.** Criterion 3 requires a positive residual from a model that predicts Pell graduation rates from student demographics and institutional features (p.6). The LPM then regresses HPP status on largely the same set of features (Table 3). By construction, residuals are close to uncorrelated with the predictors that generated them. Every HPP must pass that residual screen, and about 57% of the sample does (829/1,462). So a large part of what defines HPP status is designed to be unexplainable by these covariates. The paper contrasts the adjusted R² of 0.218 (Table 3) with the R² of 0.658 for Pell graduation rates (p.10). That comparison does not show that "traditional quantitative measures do a poor job of explaining this performance" (abstract, p.1). It shows, at least in part, that one of the outcome's three components is a residual.
- **Selectivity is omitted, even though the paper says it was tested.** On p.2 the paper names "admissions rates" among the traditional measures shown to explain HPP status poorly. Neither the covariate list (p.5) nor Table 3 contains an admission rate, test scores, or any other selectivity measure. The inventory includes Harvard, MIT, Stanford, Princeton, Caltech, and many similar institutions (Table 2). Selectivity is the obvious omitted predictor of criteria 1 and 2.
- **The access dimension is stated but never operationalized.** Figure 1 (p.4) labels "Equitable Access: Serving similar shares of Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients" as part of the framework. The text says the framework identifies institutions that "enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students" (pp.4–5). The abstract claims "low access and attainment gaps." Yet no access threshold is applied among the three criteria (p.6). HPPs in fact under-enroll Pell students compared with their catchment areas: mean Pell Ratio 0.77 (Table 1, p.7) and 24.5% Pell versus a 38% sample average (p.6). The Pell Ratio is also the strongest negative predictor of HPP status (β = −0.150, SE 0.022; Table 3, p.10).
- **Membership near the cutoffs is fragile, and the paper tests no robustness.** Criteria 1 and 3 each rest on one year (2019–20), use sample-median or zero-residual cutoffs, and report no uncertainty. The residual cutoff counts any positive residual, however small. Single-year Pell graduation rates at small institutions (e.g., Cox College, Bryan College of Health Sciences, and Mount Carmel College of Nursing in Table 2) are noisy. The paper proposes testing alternative thresholds only as future work (p.12).
- **"Practically meaningful" is judged by raw coefficient size, not a common scale.** The text calls net price, percent women, and percent borrowing too small to matter (p.10) and calls Average Pell meaningful. But Average Pell is scaled per \$1,000, and its SD among HPPs is only 0.38 thousand (Table 1). The per-percentage-point coefficients (−0.002, −0.001) imply shifts of several points over realistic ranges. The base rate is about 10% (149/1,462). Which predictors "matter" in the text reflects variable units more than substance.
- **The Discussion goes further than an associational, low-R² model can support.** The paper says institutions "do not become HPPs by simply increasing spending or enrolling different students; rather, they likely become HPPs by developing holistic, proactive, and integrated environments" (p.11). A low R² cannot tell unmeasured culture apart from measurement noise, threshold arbitrariness, omitted selectivity, or the residual construction.
- **Key parts of the prediction model are in the Online Appendix, which was not available for this review.** Those parts include the model specification, whether lagged Pell graduation rates are predictors, and the reported R² of 0.658. If lagged outcomes are included, criterion 3 measures year-over-year improvement or noise rather than performance in context. That changes what "better than expected" means.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat Table 2 as "institutions that clear these three specific 2019–20 cutoffs," not as a stable or definitive list of exemplars. Membership near the thresholds, especially at small institutions, could change with a different year or a small change in a cutoff.
- Do not read the HPP list as institutions that provide broad low-income access. No access criterion was applied. On average HPPs enroll fewer Pell students than their catchment areas would predict (Pell Ratio 0.77, Table 1, p.7).
- Discount the headline "traditional measures explain little" (R² = 0.218, Table 3). Part of the low value follows from the residual-based criterion, and selectivity was never included. It is not evidence for the "culture" interpretation on pp.11–12.
- Treat the Table 3 coefficients as descriptions of which kinds of institutions pass the screen, for example that doctoral universities pass more often (β = 0.145). They are not levers. Many of them largely reflect the construction of criteria 1 and 2.
- Ignore the HBCU coefficient (0.055, p < .10, Table 3). Only about 1 HPP is an HBCU (0.67% of 149, Table 1).
- The effective sample for inference is 1,462 institutions, not 7,310 observations. The outcome is a single, time-invariant designation repeated across 5 years.
- The earnings leg describes all Title IV entrants, not Pell graduates specifically (note 4, p.13; SAEC definition quoted on p.5). The r = 0.94 correlation offered as support (note 4) has no stated source or sample in the text.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Design and fit to the question.* This is a descriptive, classificatory study with three parts. It builds a typology from three conjoint cutoffs (RQ1), describes the institutions that pass (RQ2), and fits a linear probability model of HPP status (RQ3). For RQ1 a rules-based screen is an appropriate design. The criteria are explicit, the counts at each stage are reported (p.6), and the code is reportedly public. The conjunction yields 149 institutions, about 10% of 1,462. If the three criteria were independent, far fewer institutions would pass all three (about 1,462 × 0.40 × 0.24 × 0.57 ≈ 79). The criteria are therefore positively correlated, which makes sense because criteria 1 and 3 both key on the 2019–20 Pell graduation rate (p.6).

*The circularity problem in RQ3.* This is the most important methodological issue for readers. The paper's main substantive message, repeated in the abstract, Discussion, and Conclusion, is that observable characteristics explain little of HPP status, so unobserved organizational culture must matter. The design makes that result partly automatic. Criterion 3 is a positive residual from an OLS model of Pell graduation rates on student demographics and institutional features (p.6). The LPM regresses HPP status on those same kinds of features (the p.5 covariate list and Table 3 overlap closely). Because the prediction model is estimated on 2015–19 and applied to 2019–20, the 2019–20 residuals will not be exactly orthogonal to the 2019–20 covariates, but they should be close. The paper itself says the covariates predict Pell graduation rates well (R² = 0.658, p.10). So criterion 1, which is a threshold on that same graduation rate, is probably quite predictable on its own. The conjunction becomes hard to predict mainly because criterion 3 is added. The contrast on p.10 between 0.658 and 0.218 therefore compares a continuous outcome with a binary outcome that includes a residual by design. That comparison does not show that inputs fail to explain performance. Two further points compound this. First, an adjusted R² of 0.218 for a binary outcome with a roughly 10% base rate is not low by ordinary standards, and the paper reports no classification metric such as AUC or hit rates. Second, selectivity was never tested. On p.2 the paper lists "admissions rates" among the measures it shows to be poor explainers, but no selectivity variable appears on p.5 or in Table 3. The honest reading of RQ3 is narrower: among these IPEDS and SAEC covariates, which excluded selectivity, doctoral status and low Pell Ratio are the strongest correlates of passing the screen.

*Construct validity of the criteria.* Three points matter. (i) **Access.** Figure 1 and the surrounding text (pp.4–5) present equitable access as part of the model, and the abstract and Conclusion describe HPPs as excelling in access. None of the three operational criteria (p.6) measures access, and the resulting group has below-parity access (Pell Ratio 0.77, Table 1). The Pell Ratio then enters the LPM as a predictor with a large negative coefficient. A reader who takes "High Performing Pell" to mean "serves many low-income students well" will be misled. It means "serves its (relatively few) Pell students well by these metrics." (ii) **Completion.** A Pell graduation rate above the median is the kind of threshold that selective, well-resourced institutions pass most easily. This probably explains why the list contains many elite and flagship institutions. It sits uneasily with the Discussion's claim that the breadth of HPPs "challenges the notion that socioeconomic equity is achieved only within highly resourced or highly selective campus environments" (p.11). The paper's evidence for that claim is illustrative examples, not a comparison of HPPs with non-HPPs on resources or selectivity. (iii) **Earnings.** The SAEC Earnings Ratio covers all students who start at a school, including non-completers and non-Pell students (p.5 quote; note 4). The paper calls it "graduates' earnings" (p.5, p.11) and says it aligns with the 2019–20 graduation rates. By the standard IPEDS convention (my external knowledge, not stated in the paper), a six-year rate reported in 2019–20 refers roughly to the fall-2013 entering cohort, while the earnings are for the 2011–12 entry cohort (p.5). These are adjacent cohorts, not the same one. The gap is minor for institution-level ranking but should be noted.

*Estimation details.* The LPM pools 5 years of time-varying covariates against a single time-invariant designation (7,310 = 1,462 × 5, Table 3). It includes year and state fixed effects and clusters standard errors by institution. The clustering handles the repeated outcome correctly. The year fixed effects do little when the outcome does not vary over time. The substantive consequence is that the effective N is 1,462 and the coefficients are close to cross-sectional associations with multi-year averaged covariates. Two things are unreported: whether SAEC's Pell and URM ratios vary by year in the panel, and whether any fitted probabilities fall outside [0,1]. With a 10% base rate, the LPM is acceptable for descriptive associations. The p.10 split between "statistically but not practically significant" and "meaningful" predictors is driven by variable scaling. A \$1,000 change in Average Pell is about 2.6 SDs among HPPs (SD 0.38, Table 1), whereas a 1-point change in percent women or percent borrowing is tiny relative to realistic ranges.

*What could not be checked.* This review could not check the prediction model's specification, sample, or fit statistic (R² = 0.658, "Online Appendix Table 1"). It also could not check the LPM details the paper defers to the appendix (p.6) or anything in the data/code deposit. In particular, it cannot tell whether lagged Pell graduation rates enter the prediction model. That matters for how to interpret "better than predicted." National comparison figures in the text (38% Pell, \$4,780 average Pell, median Earnings Ratio 1.35; p.6) do not appear in any table, so they cannot be checked against a table.

**Checkable facts verified against the paper**

- Sample flow: 1,640 − 14 − 164 = 1,462 (pp.5–6). 1,640 × 5 × 46 = 377,200 cells (p.5). 1,462 × 5 = 7,310, matching Table 3 observations (p.10).
- Criterion counts: 584, 349, and 829 institutions (p.6), with 149 passing all three (p.6). 829/1,462 = 56.7% pass the residual criterion.
- Earnings cutoff: "1.54 or greater (75th percentile)" (p.6), yet 349/1,462 = 23.9% pass. The small gap from 25% may reflect ties or a percentile computed on a different universe. The text does not say which.
- Table 2 control counts: 47 Public, 99 Private NFP, 3 Private FP, totaling 149. 47/149 = 31.54%, matching "Control: Public 31.54" in Table 1 (p.7) and the "three private, for-profit institutions" in the text (p.10).
- Table 1 gap: 80.34 − 76.54 = 3.80, matching the text (p.6).
- Text-to-Table 3 checks (p.10): Pell Ratio −0.150 → "15.0 percentage points" ✓. Public −0.066 → 6.6 ✓. URM 0.032 → 3.2 ✓. Average Pell 0.030 → 3.0 ✓. Doctoral 0.145 → 14.5 ✓. Non-residential 0.078 and residential 0.044 → 7.8 and 4.4 ✓. Net price −0.003 → "0.30-point" ✓.
- **Mismatch (text vs table):** p.10 names "the share of students awarded Pell grants" as a meaningful significant predictor. Table 3 contains only the Pell Ratio, with no share-Pell variable.
- **Mismatch (text vs table):** p.10 reports "R² = 0.218". Table 3 labels 0.218 as "Adjusted R²".
- **Mismatch (table title vs sources):** Table 3's title says "2019–21", while its Sources line and the data section say 2015–16 through 2019–20 (p.5, p.10).
- **Mismatch (claim vs covariates):** p.2 lists "admissions rates" among the traditional measures shown to explain HPP status poorly. No admission-rate or selectivity variable appears in the covariate list (p.5) or in Table 3 (p.10).
- **Mismatch (framework vs operationalization):** Figure 1 (p.4) and pp.4–5 include "Equitable Access" and "enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students". The three operational criteria (p.6) contain no access criterion. HPPs' mean Pell Ratio is 0.77 (Table 1, p.7).
- **Minor mismatch:** The data section describes the Pell and loan variables as the percent of *first-year* students (p.5). The results text describes them as the share of "students enrolled at an HPP" who receive Pell or borrow (p.6).
- **Minor:** The text compares the HPP mean gap of 3.80 with "13 points nationally" (p.6). The 13 is the sample *median* gap (p.6), not a mean.
- **Minor (Discussion vs Table 3):** p.11 lists "Carnegie classifications" among characteristics with "limited explanatory power". Carnegie Doctoral has one of the two largest coefficients in Table 3 (0.145, p < .001).

  *See the correction note under Key Concerns: the two statements are compatible.*

**Interpretive judgments**

- The low R² for HPP status is substantially a consequence of defining one criterion as a residual from a model built on the same covariates, and it is not evidence for the unobserved-culture explanation.
- Omitting selectivity probably understates how much observables explain criteria 1 and 2. This is a judgment based on the composition of Table 2, not something tested in the paper.
- HPP membership is likely sensitive to the year and to the thresholds, particularly for small institutions and those near the zero-residual line. No robustness evidence is provided to settle this either way.
- The inventory is a useful starting point for sampling qualitative case studies, which is the use the authors emphasize (pp.11–12). It is weaker as a basis for recognition, funding, or benchmarking without the robustness checks above.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)


The paper describes its three immediate antecedents (Kelchen, 2017; Wright-Kim et al., 2022; Chetty, Friedman, et al., 2017) accurately enough, and its cautions about performance-based funding are well sourced. But it leaves out almost all of the literature closest to what it actually does: using "higher-than-predicted" graduation rates to find exemplar institutions, and estimating institutional value-added. It also skips the economics of selection versus college effects, critiques of Pell status as a low-income proxy, and the sociological and qualitative work on low-income students at elite and flagship campuses. It oversells the novelty of adding earnings. And in several places it describes its own sources, and its own framework, in ways that do not match what the analysis operationalizes. Readers should cite the paper for its specific conjunctive screen and its public inventory, not as the origin of the ideas behind it.

**Strengths:**

- The paper is open about its lineage. It names three antecedents explicitly (pp. 2–5, Figure 1 p. 4) and states which criterion comes from which source (p. 6). That makes its intellectual debts easy to trace.
- It gives a fair, concrete account of Bassett (2025), the nearest contemporaneous comparison. Note 1 (p. 13) spells out Bassett's "equity engine" thresholds and how HPP differs.
- It flags the limits of SAEC openly. Note 4 (p. 13) says the Earnings Ratio "measure[s] post-graduate earnings, not intergenerational social mobility like Chetty, Friedman et al. (2017)," and that SAEC earnings cover all Title IV students rather than Pell recipients. Note 10 (p. 13) flags the geographic-coverage problems with SAEC measures.
- The policy discussion (p. 12) cites empirical work on how performance-based funding penalizes high-need institutions (Ortagus et al., 2023; Boland, 2025; Zerquera & Ziskin, 2020), and it cautions against using HPP for accountability.
- It brings a student-affairs framework, ecological validation (Kitchen et al., 2021; Kezar et al., 2024), into a largely economics-of-education question. In principle that is a useful bridge between the quantitative and organizational traditions.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The method's own tradition is missing.** Criterion 3 compares each institution's actual Pell graduation rate with a regression-predicted rate (p. 6). The paper presents this as extending Wright-Kim et al. (2022). In fact, "actual vs. expected graduation rate" is a decades-old approach: Astin's input–environment–outcome work, Kuh et al.'s Project DEEP, Education Trust's peer-predicted rates, the graduation-rate-performance measures in US News and Washington Monthly, and the college value-added literature. None of this is cited. Its known pitfalls go unmentioned as well: rankings shift with covariate choice, estimates are noisy and regress to the mean for small institutions, and residuals mix institutional effect with unobserved selection.
- **The earnings novelty is oversold.** Note 6 (p. 13) says considering earnings "introduces a dimension of institutional performance that has been absent from prior work in this area." Combining access, completion, and post-college earnings is already the core of Chetty et al.'s mobility-rate framework, the Postsecondary Value Commission's "equitable value" framework, Third Way's economic-mobility and price-to-earnings work, and the earnings-performance measures in college rankings. What is new is the use of the 2025 SAEC Earnings Ratio (p. 4). That is a data novelty, not a conceptual one.
- **The paper misdescribes its earnings source.** It repeatedly calls the Earnings Ratio a measure of *graduates'* earnings ("higher-than-expected earnings among graduates," p. 2; "graduates earn more than expected," p. 4; "all Title IV graduates," Note 4 p. 13). But its own quotation of the SAEC manual (p. 5) says the ratio "compares the median earnings of students who **start** at a school." The measure is also described as "8 years after entry" (p. 4). To my knowledge, College Scorecard's institution-level earnings measured years after entry cover entrants regardless of completion. That would mean the earnings screen partly rewards completion a second time.
- **The "access" pillar is claimed but not operationalized.** The conceptual model says HPP emerges from "the intersection of three domain measures of success: access to college, completion of a degree, and post-graduation earnings" (p. 4). It claims to identify institutions that "enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students" (pp. 4–5), and Figure 1 (p. 4) brackets "Equitable Access: Serving similar shares of Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients." None of the three selection criteria on p. 6 involves access. HPPs average a Pell Ratio of 0.77 and 24.52% of students awarded Pell (Table 1, p. 7), against a sample average of 38% (p. 6). And the Pell Ratio is the strongest negative predictor of HPP status (−0.150, Table 3, p. 10). Against Bassett (2025), which imposes a ≥34% Pell floor (Note 1, p. 13), and SAEC's own access axis, HPP is a success-conditional-on-enrollment screen, not an access-and-success screen.
- **Critiques of Pell as a low-income proxy go unengaged.** A body of work (e.g., Tebbs & Turner, 2005; Delisle, 2017 — see Guidance for certainty) documents what Pell status actually captures. The paper leans on Pell-vs-non-Pell gaps (criterion 1) without discussing why those gaps are hard to compare across institutions. The non-Pell group mixes middle-income non-filers with affluent students in proportions that vary sharply by institution. Pell receipt depends on cost of attendance, FAFSA filing, and dependency status. IPEDS Pell graduation rates cover only first-time, full-time cohorts. The same gap tells you different things at Harvard and at a regional public.
- **Evidence that cuts against the paper's interpretations is largely missing.** (a) Causal evidence that spending raises completion (e.g., Deming & Walters; Webber & Ehrenberg; Bound, Lovenheim & Turner) sits awkwardly with the claim that "institutions do not become HPPs by simply increasing spending" (p. 11), which rests on non-significant cross-sectional coefficients. (b) Selection-versus-effect work (Dale & Krueger; Mountjoy & Hickman; Chetty, Deming & Friedman's Ivy-Plus study) bears directly on reading high earnings ratios at Harvard, MIT, and Stanford (named p. 7) as institutional performance. (c) Sociological ethnographies of low-income students at elite and flagship campuses (Jack, *The Privileged Poor*; Armstrong & Hamilton, *Paying for the Party*) show that high completion can coexist with class-marginalizing climates. That undercuts the inference that HPPs "likely" have validating environments (p. 11).
- **Several citations are loosely matched to the claims they support.** Card (1999), a study of the causal return to schooling, is cited for institutions as "engines of economic opportunity" (p. 3). Hoxby and Turner (2015), a note on what high-achieving low-income students know about college, is cited for low-income students graduating at lower rates (p. 2) and as a "long-standing critique of stratification" (p. 11). Wright-Kim et al. (2022) is used in both directions: as showing that institutional characteristics explain "a substantial amount of variance" (p. 3), and as showing they "only partially explain" Pell completion (p. 11). There are also smaller inconsistencies. Figure 1 credits "Wright-Kim et al., 2019" (p. 4), while the text and reference list use 2022 (p. 15). A Kezar et al. (2024) quotation is cited to "p. 1" (p. 2), but the reference runs pp. 229–242 (p. 14). Several works are cited as working papers although published versions exist (e.g., Chetty, Friedman, et al., 2017).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **When citing this paper,** cite it for (i) the specific three-way conjunctive screen (p. 6), (ii) an early empirical use of the 2025 ACE/Carnegie SAEC data (p. 4, Note 6), and (iii) the public 149-institution inventory (Table 2, pp. 8–9; replication materials at the openICPSR DOI, p. 13). Do not cite it as originating the idea of combining access, completion, and earnings, or the idea of flagging colleges that beat predicted graduation rates. Those belong to predecessors (next bullets).
- **Companion readings on the residual/exemplar method** (high confidence these exist; check the exact titles): Astin (1997), "How 'good' is your institution's retention rate?" (*Research in Higher Education*). Kuh, Kinzie, Schuh, Whitt & Associates (2005), *Student Success in College* (Project DEEP), which used higher-than-predicted graduation and engagement to pick institutions and then did the case studies this paper calls for as future work. Cunha & Miller (2014, *Economics of Education Review*) on the possibilities and limits of higher-education value-added. Kane & Staiger (2002, *Journal of Economic Perspectives*) on how imprecise single-year measures produce spurious "top performers," especially among small units. Table 1 (p. 7) shows 36.24% of HPPs are small institutions.
- **Companion readings on combining access, completion, and earnings** (high confidence on the first; moderate on the rest): Chetty, Friedman, Saez, Turner & Yagan, published as "Income segregation and intergenerational mobility across colleges in the United States" (*QJE*, 2020). Its access × success "mobility rate" makes explicit the trade-off that shows up here as the negative Pell Ratio coefficient. The Postsecondary Value Commission's 2021 "Equitable Value" report (IHEP). Third Way's economic-mobility and price-to-earnings work. The Washington Monthly and US News social-mobility metrics, whose Pell-graduation and earnings-performance components (from my recollection, worth verifying) closely resemble HPP criteria 1–3.
- **On what "Pell" measures** (moderate confidence on exact titles): Tebbs & Turner (2005, *Change*), a caution about using Pell recipient data to measure low-income enrollment. Delisle (2017, Brookings), on the "Pell Grant proxy" as a flawed measure. For causal evidence on Pell itself, relevant to the "return on Pell dollars" argument on p. 12: Denning, Marx & Turner (2019, *AEJ: Applied*), and, as I recall it, Eng & Matsudaira (2021, *Journal of Labor Economics*). Keep in mind that an institution's average Pell award reflects the need profile and enrollment intensity of its Pell recipients. So the "Average Pell" coefficient (0.030 per \$1,000, Table 3, p. 10) is not a measure of institutional aid policy.
- **On selection vs. institutional effects,** which matters before reading high earnings ratios as performance: Dale & Krueger (2002, 2014); Mountjoy & Hickman (NBER, 2021) on college value-added; Chetty, Deming & Friedman (2023) on Ivy-Plus admissions. The SAEC ratio adjusts for education, race/ethnicity, and geography (p. 5) but, as described, not for academic preparation.
- **On the qualitative and organizational side:** Jack (2019), *The Privileged Poor*; Armstrong & Hamilton (2013), *Paying for the Party*; Bastedo & Jaquette (2011, *EEPA*) on stratification dynamics. From psychology, Walton & Yeager (2020, *Current Directions*) on "seed and soil," and Walton et al. (2023, *Science*) on where belonging interventions work. These give the "context affordances" idea a quantitative footing that the paper's ecological-validation argument lacks. On comprehensive, coordinated supports with causal evidence (mostly community-college settings): Weiss et al. (2019) on CUNY ASAP; Evans et al. (2020, *JPAM*) on Stay the Course.
- **On performance funding** (beyond the paper's citations): the systematic review by Ortagus, Kelchen, Rosinger & Voorhees (2020, *EEPA*). Gándara & Rutherford (2018, *Research in Higher Education*) on equity premiums in PBF formulas. Many PBF formulas already reward Pell completion, so HPP-like metrics are not as far from accountability use as p. 12 suggests.
- **Before repeating these claims:** (a) Check the SAEC technical manual on whether the Earnings Ratio covers graduates or all entrants, and whether the 75th-percentile cut (1.54, p. 6) is "similar to" SAEC's own thresholds. (b) Check Kelchen (2017). It is a short Brookings blog post, and the median/gap screen called "Kelchen's (2017) classification" (p. 6) appears to be the authors' own operationalization; to my recollection, the post did not propose a formal classification. (c) Check Bassett's (2025) thresholds as summarized in Note 1 (p. 13). (d) Check the r = 0.94 Pell/non-Pell program-earnings correlation in Note 4 (p. 13), which gives no source or computation.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*How the paper positions itself.* The paper frames its contribution as "unifying" three works (p. 2, p. 5, p. 10): Kelchen's (2017) descriptive look at the first IPEDS Pell graduation data, Wright-Kim et al.'s (2022) regression of Pell completion on institutional characteristics, and Chetty, Friedman, et al.'s (2017) Mobility Report Cards. It adds the 2025 SAEC as the earnings source (p. 4) and ecological validation (Kitchen et al., 2021) as the interpretive lens (p. 2, p. 11). This framing is transparent, but it is narrow in ways that affect how readers should value the contribution. One of the three pillars is a blog post. The Chetty lineage is invoked but not used methodologically: HPP uses neither parent-income data nor a mobility-rate construct, and Note 4 concedes the SAEC measure is not intergenerational mobility. Yet Figure 1 still labels the earnings circle "High Economic Mobility" (p. 4). The most substantive methodological move, criterion 3, has a long history the paper does not acknowledge.

*The missing value-added and exemplar tradition.* The idea of benchmarking an institution's graduation rate against a covariate-predicted expectation, then treating over-performers as exemplars worth studying qualitatively, is well established in higher education. Astin's work on "expected" retention, Project DEEP (Kuh et al., 2005), Education Trust's peer-comparison tools and gap reports, and the graduation-rate-performance components of US News and Washington Monthly all precede this paper. So does an economics literature on college value-added, which warns that residual-based rankings are sensitive to specification and contaminated by selection. The broader "positive deviance" / "beating the odds" design (in health services research and in K-12 "positive outlier" studies) is the natural methodological home for this paper, and neither the term nor its literature appears. This matters for readers in two ways. First, the novelty claim shrinks. Second, the paper's key interpretive leap is exactly what that literature cautions against. It reads the unexplained variance in HPP status (adjusted R² = 0.218, Table 3, p. 10) as pointing to "organizational culture, values, student-centered practices, and networks of support" (p. 11) and to ecological validation. Residuals and low R² values contain noise, measurement error in small Pell cohorts, and unobserved student selection, not only culture. Moreover, criterion 3 is itself defined as a residual from a model using largely the same covariates. So the low explanatory power of those covariates for HPP status is partly built in by construction. That weakens the claim that the finding "aligns with" Wright-Kim et al. (p. 11) as substantive corroboration. (Full evaluation of this belongs to the methods review; I raise it because it bears on how the paper uses the literature.)

*Selectivity and the Wright-Kim link.* On p. 2 the paper says it shows that traditional measures "identified in prior works (e.g., … admissions rates …; Wright-Kim et al., 2022)" poorly explain HPP status. On p. 3 it reports that Wright-Kim et al. found selectivity and SAT scores among the characteristics tied to Pell completion. Yet no admissions-rate or test-score variable appears in the covariate list on p. 5, in Table 1 (p. 7), or in Table 3 (p. 10). The prediction model for criterion 3 is in the Online Appendix, which I could not check. As far as the printed paper shows, then, the strongest predictors from the paper's main antecedent are not in the models used to argue that "traditional measures" fail. That is a gap between how the literature is characterized and how it is used.

*Access.* The paper's positioning against Bassett (2025, Note 1) and its "unified view" of access, completion, and earnings (p. 4) imply that HPP captures access. It does not: none of the three criteria on p. 6 uses the Pell Ratio or Pell share. The outcome is predictable from the Chetty et al. access/success trade-off. The HPP set under-enrolls Pell students relative to its geographies (mean Pell Ratio 0.77, Table 1, p. 7) and includes the most selective private universities (p. 7). The Discussion's claim that HPP breadth "challenges the notion that socioeconomic equity is achieved only within highly resourced or highly selective campus environments" (p. 11) should be read alongside that fact. The Discussion does acknowledge the negative Pell Ratio association (p. 11), and the inventory does include some high-access publics (e.g., several California State University campuses, Florida International University, Stony Brook; Table 2, pp. 8–9). But readers wanting an access-and-success list should also look at Bassett's equity engines and SAEC's high-access/high-earnings cells.

*Pell as a proxy.* Criterion 1 treats the Pell/non-Pell gap as a comparable equity measure across institutions (median gap threshold of 13 points, p. 6; HPP mean gap 3.80, Table 1, p. 7). That comparison needs the literature on what Pell status captures. At a high-sticker-price institution, many middle-income students qualify for Pell; at a low-cost one, fewer do. Non-filers fall into "non-Pell." And the composition of "non-Pell" ranges from nearly all affluent to largely modest-income. A small gap at a low-price regional public and a small gap at an elite private are different phenomena. The paper does not raise this, although the elements are in its own reference list (Nichols, 2015; Whistle & Hiler, 2018 are cited only as sources for covariates or context, p. 2, p. 5).

*Adjacent literatures that change the reading.*

- Economics: Research on college effects versus selection bears on criterion 2. Readers should treat high earnings ratios at the most selective HPPs as partly reflecting who enrolls; the SAEC ratio adjusts for education, race/ethnicity, and geography but not academic preparation (p. 5). Causal spending studies bear on the Discussion's claim about spending (p. 11).
- Sociology: Qualitative work on class inside elite and flagship institutions directly addresses the paper's inference that high, equal completion signals validating climates. It suggests completion parity and a validating experience can come apart.
- Psychology: The social-belonging and "seed and soil" literature offers experimentally grounded evidence that institutional context moderates low-income and minoritized student success. That is the claim the paper makes via ecological validation, but it would give the claim a quantitative anchor the paper lacks.
- Policy: The 2025 federal reconciliation law is cited only for Pell changes (Zampini, 2025, p. 12). To my recollection, the same law also created program-level earnings accountability tests (worth verifying), which makes earnings-based institutional screens like HPP more policy-relevant, and more open to accountability uses, than the paper's caution on p. 12 suggests.

*Checkable facts verified against the paper:*

- The three antecedents are named on p. 2 and p. 3–5, and in Figure 1's source line ("Informed by Chetty, Friedman et al., 2017; Kelchen, 2017; Wright-Kim et al., 2019; and others," p. 4). The reference list dates Wright-Kim et al. to 2022 (p. 15).
- Kelchen (2017) appears in the references as a Brookings Brown Center Chalkboard blog post (p. 14). The text calls it "Kelchen's (2017) classification" (p. 6).
- The selection criteria (p. 6): Pell graduation rate above the sample median of 50% and a Pell/non-Pell gap under 13 points (584 institutions); Earnings Ratio ≥ 1.54, the 75th percentile (349 institutions); higher-than-predicted Pell graduation rate (829 institutions). All three together: 149 HPPs. None of the criteria uses the Pell Ratio.
- HPP means (Table 1, p. 7): Pell graduation rate 76.54; gap 3.80; Earnings Ratio 1.89; URM Ratio 0.97; Pell Ratio 0.77; students awarded Pell 24.52%; small institutions 36.24%. The text gives a sample average Pell share of 38% (p. 6).
- Table 3 (p. 10): Pell Ratio −0.150***; Average Pell 0.030**; Carnegie Doctoral 0.145***; no expenditure coefficient significant at p < .05; adjusted R² 0.218; N = 7,310. The p. 10 text cites R² = 0.658 for the Pell graduation prediction model in Online Appendix Table 1. The Online Appendix was not available to me and could not be checked.
- The paper's own SAEC quotation says the Earnings Ratio "compares the median earnings of students who start at a school" (p. 5). Elsewhere it calls the ratio graduates' earnings (p. 2, p. 4, Note 4 p. 13).
- The novelty claims appear on p. 4 ("among the first to leverage SAEC data") and in Note 6 (p. 13) (earnings "absent from prior work in this area").
- A Kezar et al. (2024) quotation is cited to "p. 1" (p. 2); the reference gives pp. 229–242 (p. 14).
- The admissions rate appears among "traditional measures" on p. 2, but no admissions-rate or SAT variable appears in the p. 5 covariate list, Table 1, or Table 3.
- The reference list has about 45 entries. None addresses institutional value-added or graduation-rate residual methods, positive-deviance or exemplar designs, critiques of Pell as a proxy, or selection-versus-effect estimates of college quality.

*Interpretive judgments / external-literature recollections:*

- My judgment that the residual-based exemplar tradition (Astin; Kuh et al./DEEP; Education Trust; ranking "performance" measures; college value-added) is the paper's true methodological lineage rests on my knowledge of the field. The specific works named are ones I am confident exist. Exact titles, years, and venues should be verified before citing, especially where I flagged moderate confidence (Tebbs & Turner 2005; Delisle 2017; Eng & Matsudaira 2021; Gándara & Rutherford 2018; Mountjoy & Hickman 2021).
- The claim that College Scorecard institution-level "years after entry" earnings include non-completers comes from my understanding of Scorecard documentation, not from this paper. Readers should confirm it against the SAEC technical manual.
- My recollection that the Washington Monthly and US News social-mobility metrics include Pell graduation performance, Pell/non-Pell comparisons, and earnings-performance components is from memory, and the details have changed over the years.
- I cannot verify that Kelchen (2017) found what p. 3 reports (high Pell graduation rates concentrated at selective, low-Pell institutions). It is consistent with my general recollection of early IPEDS Pell data. Likewise, I cannot verify Wright-Kim et al.'s (2022) specific findings or Bassett's (2025) thresholds (Note 1) beyond the paper's summaries.
- My recollection that the ecological validation model came out of research on the Thompson Scholars Learning Communities (a Nebraska scholarship-linked program also studied by economists) is uncertain and worth verifying. If correct, it offers a ready bridge between the qualitative and experimental literatures that the paper does not use.
- My recollection that the 2025 reconciliation law included earnings-based accountability provisions is moderate-confidence and worth verifying.
- The overall rating reflects my judgment that the omissions sit on the paper's central methodological and interpretive claims, not at the periphery. I have less visibility into very recent (2025–2026) work that directly uses SAEC data or HPP-like screens. Some near-contemporaneous work may exist that neither the paper nor I identify.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)


The paper is short, readable, and transcribes its own table numbers accurately: every Table 1 and Table 3 value quoted in the Results matches the exhibit, and Table 2 lists exactly 149 institutions. The problem is fidelity of argument. The abstract, Figure 1, the conceptual model, and the Discussion/Conclusion describe HPPs as excelling on *access* (low access gaps, enrolling large Pell shares), but none of the three operational criteria measures access. The paper's own Table 1 (Pell Ratio 0.77; 24.5% Pell vs. a 38% sample average) shows HPPs enroll *fewer* Pell students than expected, and the Pell Ratio is the strongest negative predictor of HPP status in Table 3. The Discussion also contradicts the Results on which predictors matter, and several headline comparisons restate the selection rule rather than reporting findings.

**Strengths:**

- Transcription from exhibits to prose is accurate. All 18 Table 1 values and all 8 Table 3 coefficients quoted in the Results (pp. 6, 10) match the tables to rounding, and the unit conversions for financial variables (Table 3 note: "scaled by 1,000") are applied correctly (e.g., Average Pell β = 0.030 becomes "3.0-point increase" per \$1,000, p. 10).
- The sample arithmetic holds together. 1,640 × 5 × 46 = 377,200 (p. 5), 1,640 − 14 − 164 = 1,462 (pp. 5–6), and 1,462 × 5 = 7,310, the Table 3 observation count (p. 10).
- Table 2 (pp. 8–9) is complete and consistent with the text. It has 149 rows (114 on p. 8, 35 on p. 9); the two "University of St Thomas" entries are distinct (MN and TX). Its control counts (47 Public, 99 Private NFP, 3 Private FP) reproduce Table 1's 31.54% public (47/149) and the text's "three private, for-profit institutions" (p. 10).
- The Empirical Strategy (p. 6) states the three operational criteria plainly, gives the count meeting each (584, 349, 829), and flags that Pell graduation rates enter two of the three criteria. That is a helpful, honest note.
- Table 3's interpretation paragraph (p. 10) walks through coefficient magnitudes in plain language and correctly reminds readers that the model explains "less than 22%" of variance.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The abstract misstates the identification criteria.** It says HPPs have "high Pell graduation rates, low access and attainment gaps between Pell and non-Pell students, and relatively high earnings" (p. 1). No operational criterion measures an access gap (p. 6). The abstract also omits the better-than-predicted Pell graduation rate criterion, which is one of the three filters and removes 633 of 1,462 institutions (829 pass, p. 6).
- **The access dimension runs through the framing but is never operationalized, and the data point the other way.** Figure 1 (p. 4) wraps all three circles in an "Equitable Access: Serving similar shares of Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients" bracket. The conceptual model promises to identify institutions that "(a) enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students" (pp. 4–5). The LPM is described as explaining "high access, completion, and post-graduation earnings outcomes" (p. 6), and the Conclusion says HPPs "excel in access, completion, and post-graduation earnings" (p. 12). Yet Table 1 shows a mean Pell Ratio of 0.77 (p. 7), about 23% below expected Pell enrollment. The text reports the URM Ratio (0.97) from the same block of Table 1 but never mentions the Pell Ratio row.
- **The Discussion contradicts the Results.** Results (p. 10) calls student demographics (Pell Ratio, URM Ratio) and doctoral status "statistically significant and meaningful predictors." The Discussion (p. 11) then says "student demographics, and Carnegie classifications—have limited explanatory power." Carnegie Doctoral (0.145***) and Pell Ratio (−0.150***) are the two largest coefficients in Table 3.
- **Several headline comparisons are true by construction and mix means with medians.** "Remarkably high Pell graduation rates (76.5% … compared to a national sample median of 50%)" and "substantially higher earnings ratios (1.89 compared to a sample median of 1.35)" (p. 6) compare HPP *means* to sample *medians* on variables the HPPs were *selected* on (>50%, <13-point gap, ≥1.54). Note 2 itself argues medians and means are not interchangeable in these skewed data.
- **The Table 3 prose mislabels the key variable.** The text says "the share of students awarded Pell grants" is a meaningful predictor and that likelihood falls "as the number of Pell Grant recipients enrolled on a campus increases" (p. 10). Table 3 contains neither a share nor a count, only the Pell Ratio, a geography-relative index.
- **The "practical significance" sorting is not supported by the coefficients' scale** (see Interpretive judgments). Net price, which is labeled "too small" to matter, has a larger per-SD association than the average Pell award, which is labeled "meaningful."
- **Production and consistency lapses survived.** Table 3's title says "2019–21" while its Sources line and the text say 2015–16 through 2019–20 (pp. 5, 6, 10). Figure 1 cites "Wright-Kim et al., 2019" while the text and references say 2022. The text reports "R² = 0.218" where Table 3 reports adjusted R². Table 1's BEA region shares sum to 99.33% (148 of 149 institutions).
- **Table 1 has no comparison column.** RQ2 asks about the "unique characteristics" of HPPs (p. 5), but Table 1 reports HPPs only. Every contrast in the text (38% Pell share, \$4,780 average Pell award, 1.35 median earnings ratio, "13 points nationally") uses figures that appear in no exhibit.
- **Key design details are only in the Online Appendix, which I could not check.** These include the prediction model, its R² of 0.658 (p. 10), and the LPM specification. The text never explains how HPP status, which is defined from 2019–20 data only, becomes the outcome in a five-year panel with year fixed effects (Table 3: 7,310 = 1,462 × 5).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Must read:** the Empirical Strategy (p. 6). It is the only place where the three operational criteria are stated correctly, and they differ from the abstract and from Figure 1. Read it before citing what an "HPP" is.
- **Must read:** Table 1 (p. 7), including the Pell Ratio row (0.77) and "Students Awarded Pell (%)" (24.52) that the prose passes over. HPPs are high-completion, high-earnings, small-gap institutions that enroll *below-expected* shares of Pell students. They are not high-access institutions.
- **Must read:** Table 3 (p. 10). Quote coefficients from the table, not the prose; the prose names the Pell variable wrong (see audit). Treat the model as descriptive correlation in a sample where about 10% of institutions (149/1,462) are HPPs.
- **Do not quote the comparisons** "76.5% vs. 50%," "1.89 vs. 1.35," or "3.80 vs. 13 points" (p. 6) as findings. The selection criteria guarantee these gaps, and each compares a mean to a median.
- **Skim or skip:** the Introduction and Background (pp. 1–3), and Implications (pp. 11–12), which restate the three criteria several times and contain no data. The Discussion's causal-sounding claims ("institutions do not become HPPs by simply increasing spending or enrolling different students," p. 11) go beyond an LPM with an adjusted R² of 0.218.
- **Table 2 is printed landscape across two pages.** Alphabetical order runs down each column on p. 8 and then continues on p. 9 (Duquesne on p. 8 is followed by Embry-Riddle on p. 9). Institutions beginning with "The" are filed under T.
- **Figures you cannot verify from this article:** the 38% and \$4,780 sample averages, the 1.35 sample median, the "roughly 3%" HBCU and "<3%" Land Grant national shares, the 0.658 prediction R², and all Online Appendix content.

**Detailed Commentary:**

#### Organization and navigability

The structure is conventional and short: roughly 3 pages of framing, 1 page of data and methods, 4 pages of results (half of which is Table 2), and 2.5 pages of discussion. The load-bearing material is concentrated on pp. 6–7 and p. 10: the three criteria, Table 1, and Table 3. The rest is framing that restates the criteria about six times (p. 2, p. 3, pp. 4–5, p. 6 twice, p. 11). The restatements do not agree with each other (see below), so a reader who stops at any one of them gets a different definition of HPP. The research questions (p. 5) are clear, but RQ2 ("unique characteristics") cannot be answered by Table 1 as designed, because it has no non-HPP comparison. The paper answers it only through unexhibited sample averages quoted in prose.

Methodological detail is thin in the main text. The prediction model's specification, fit, and covariates, as well as the LPM specification, are deferred to the Online Appendix (pp. 6, 10). The Supplemental Material was not available to me and could not be checked. The main text leaves several reader questions open:

- how a status defined only for 2019–20 serves as the outcome in a 2015–16 to 2019–20 panel with year fixed effects (Table 3);
- how 14 institutions could have "only one year of data" (p. 5) after the sample was already restricted to institutions reporting Pell graduation rates "in each year" (p. 5);
- which sample (1,640 or 1,462) defines the "sample (national) median" (p. 6).

#### Abstract and criteria fidelity: exact wording by page

- **Abstract (p. 1):** "having high Pell graduation rates, low access and attainment gaps between Pell and non-Pell students, and relatively high earnings after graduation."
- **Introduction (p. 2):** "Pell graduation rates above the national median and below-median gaps in graduation rates between Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients; higher-than-predicted Pell graduation rates given institutional features; and substantially higher-than-expected earnings among graduates." *(Matches p. 6.)*
- **Figure 1 (p. 4):** three circles ("High and Equitable Completion Rates," "High Performance within Context," "High Economic Mobility"), all bracketed by "Equitable Access: Serving similar shares of Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients."
- **Conceptual model (pp. 4–5):** HPPs "(a) enroll a large share of Pell-eligible students, graduate them at higher-than-median rates, and have low or nonexistent completion gaps … (b) perform better than expected … and (c) provide graduates with opportunities for upward mobility through relatively high post-graduation earnings."
- **Empirical Strategy (p. 6):** "having Pell graduation rates above the national median and below-median gaps between Pell and non-Pell Grant recipients; higher-than-predicted Pell graduation rates given institutional features; and higher-than-expected earnings."
- **Discussion (p. 11):** "(a) exhibit both high and equitable completion rates … (b) outperform their predicted graduation rates … (c) produce graduates with higher-than-expected earnings." *(Matches p. 6.)*

The p. 2, p. 6, and p. 11 statements agree with each other. The abstract, Figure 1, and the pp. 4–5 conceptual text each add an access component that is never implemented. The abstract also drops criterion (b). Two further terminology slips compound this:

- **"Earnings after graduation" is not what the measure captures.** The abstract, p. 2, and p. 6 describe the Earnings Ratio as graduates' earnings, but the paper's own quotation of the SAEC definition (p. 5) says it "compares the median earnings of students who start at a school," measured "8 years after entry." That population includes non-completers.
- **"Mobility" is not what the measure captures.** Figure 1 labels the earnings circle "High Economic Mobility," while Note 4 (p. 13) says the SAEC measures "post-graduate earnings, not intergenerational social mobility."
